interpretation: A prespecified sex-specific analysis reported that rosuvastatin reduced cardiovascular events in women (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.37-0.80, P=0.002) and in men (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.45-0.73). No formal rosuvastatin-specific sex-by-treatment interaction test was located in the reviewed sources, so AMIRA does not report a drug-specific significance conclusion.
exact_passage: relative risk reduction in women (hazard ratio, 0.54; 95% confidence interval, 0.37 to 0.80; P=0.002) and men (hazard ratio, 0.58; 95% confidence interval, 0.45 to 0.73; P<0.001). In women, there was significant reduction in revascularization/unstable angina and nonsignificant reductions in other components of the primary end point.

endpoint: Major vascular events per 1.0 mmol/L LDL-C reduction
interpretation: Class-level meta-analysis (27 statin trials, 46,675 women): proportional reduction in major vascular events was similar in women (RR 0.84) and men (RR 0.78), heterogeneity-by-sex p=0.33. This is class-level evidence, not specific to rosuvastatin.
exact_passage: The proportional reductions per 1.0 mmol/L reduction in LDL cholesterol in major vascular events were similar overall for women (rate ratio [RR] 0.84, 99% CI 0.78-0.91) and men (RR 0.78, 99% CI 0.75-0.81, adjusted p value for heterogeneity by sex=0.33) and also for those women and men at less than 10% predicted 5 year absolute cardiovascular risk (adjusted heterogeneity p=0.11).

interpretation: Class-level meta-analysis reported no adverse effect on cancer incidence or non-cardiovascular mortality for either sex. No rosuvastatin-specific sex-stratified adverse-event breakdown (e.g. muscle symptoms) was located in the reviewed sources.
exact_passage: No adverse effect on rates of cancer incidence or non-cardiovascular mortality was noted for either sex. These net benefits translated into all-cause mortality reductions with statin therapy for both women (RR 0.91, 99% CI 0.84-0.99) and men (RR 0.90, 99% CI 0.86-0.95; adjusted heterogeneity p=0.43).

endpoint: Worsening heart failure event or cardiovascular death
interpretation: A prespecified DAPA-HF analysis reported that dapagliflozin reduced the primary outcome to a similar extent in women (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.59-1.06) and men (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.63-0.85), with a formal sex-by-treatment interaction p=0.67. This is a drug-specific comparison, so 'no significant sex difference' is supported for dapagliflozin.
exact_passage: a similar extent in both men and women (hazard ratios, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.63-0.85] and 0.79 [95% CI, 0.59-1.06], respectively; P for interaction = .67). Consistent benefits were observed for the components of the primary outcome and all-cause mortality.

endpoint: Serious adverse events and study-drug discontinuation
effect_measure: Reported separately by sex (within-sex vs placebo)
interpretation: Serious adverse events and study-drug discontinuation were reported separately by sex, and were not more frequent with dapagliflozin than placebo in either men or women. That is a within-sex comparison against placebo; no formal between-sex safety comparison or interaction test was reported in the reviewed source, so no between-sex safety difference is claimed either way.
exact_passage: Study drug discontinuation and serious adverse events were not more frequent in the dapagliflozin group than in the placebo group in either men or women.

endpoint: Reached target office blood pressure at 38 weeks
interpretation: In this postmenopausal women-only trial, 71.7% of the valsartan-based regimen group and 71.4% of the amlodipine-based regimen group reached target office blood pressure. This compares treatment arms within women; it is not a comparison between women and men.
exact_passage: At the end of the study, the overall percentage of the patients reaching target office BP (<140/90 mm Hg) was identical in both groups (71.7% vs 71.4%; P=not significant).

interpretation: Peripheral edema was reported in 14.3% of the valsartan-based regimen group and 77.4% of the amlodipine-based regimen group (P<0.001) in this single postmenopausal women-only study. The result is treatment-arm evidence within women, not a between-sex safety comparison.
exact_passage: AE was peripheral edema, affecting 77.4% and 14.3% patients in the amlodipine and valsartan treatment groups, respectively.

interpretation: A post hoc DIG analysis found a statistically significant interaction between sex and digoxin for all-cause mortality. Among women, mortality was 33.1% with digoxin and 28.9% with placebo, an absolute difference of 4.2 percentage points; the unadjusted women-only confidence interval included no difference. This analysis identifies an association in a post hoc subgroup and does not establish a menopause-specific effect.
exact_passage: higher risk of death among women (adjusted hazard ratio for the comparison with placebo, 1.23; 95 percent confidence interval, 1.02 to 1.47), but it had no significant effect among men (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.93; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.85 to 1.02; P=0.014 for the interaction). The effect of digoxin therapy differs between men and women.
why_it_matters: A historical analysis found higher mortality among women assigned digoxin. This signal should not be missed, but it does not by itself determine treatment for an individual patient.

endpoint: Total worsening heart failure events and cardiovascular mortality
interpretation: DECISION targeted a low serum digoxin concentration of 0.5-0.9 ng/mL. The primary-outcome treatment effect did not differ significantly between women and men (interaction P=0.61). The overall primary outcome was also not statistically significant (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.61-1.07; P=0.133).
exact_passage: primary endpoint between women and men (rate ratio digoxin versus placebo: 0.71 and 0.85, respectively, P value for interaction 0.61) (Fig. 3 ).

interpretation: The publication reports that low-dose digoxin was safe in the 284 women studied. A formal between-sex adverse-event interaction estimate was not located, so AMIRA does not infer equivalent safety between women and men.
exact_passage: In the present study, low-dose digoxin was safe in the 284 women studied, and a similar signal was also seen in 247 women who received (low-dose) digitoxin in DIGIT-HF 9 . These data therefore provide reassurance regarding the use of (low-dose) digoxin in women.

effect_measure: Incidence by sex and adjusted odds
interpretation: In a pooled analysis of 22 oral d,l-sotalol trials (3,135 patients), torsade de pointes developed in 4.1% (33/799) of women and 1.9% (44/2336) of men (P < 0.001). After adjustment for reported risk factors, women had approximately threefold greater odds of developing torsades de pointes than men. Torsade de pointes is a potentially life-threatening rhythm disturbance, and female sex was an independent risk factor within the analysed population. This is a historical pooled clinical-trial analysis of d,l-sotalol and is not an individual treatment recommendation.
exact_passage: TdP developed in 44 (1.9%) of 2336 men and in 33 (4.1%) of 799 women (P < .001). After adjustment for these risk factors, women had threefold greater odds of developing TdP than men.
signal_headline: Women experienced a higher rate of torsades de pointes during sotalol treatment
signal_summary: 4.1% (33/799) women vs 1.9% (44/2336) men · P < 0.001 · ~3-fold higher adjusted odds in women
why_it_matters: Torsade de pointes is a potentially life-threatening rhythm disturbance, and the study identified female sex as an independent risk factor within the analyzed population.
cautions: Individual risk also depends on dose, renal function, heart failure, arrhythmia history, and other factors

effect_measure: Fracture incidence by sex (drug vs placebo)
interpretation: In PROactive (5,238 patients; mean follow-up 34.5 months), bone-fracture incidence in female participants was 5.1% (44/870) with pioglitazone versus 2.5% (23/905) with placebo. No increase in fracture incidence was observed in men (1.7% vs 2.1%). The majority of fractures in women were nonvertebral, involving the lower limb and distal upper limb. This is a within-trial sex-stratified safety signal from the prescribing information; a formal between-sex interaction test was not located, so AMIRA reports the higher fracture incidence in women without asserting an interaction statistic. Menopause status is not inferred and this is not a treatment recommendation.
exact_passage: During a mean follow-up of 34.5 months, the incidence of bone fracture in females was 5.1% (44/870) for pioglitazone tablets versus 2.5% (23/905) for placebo. No increase in the incidence of fracture was observed in men treated with pioglitazone tablets (1.7%) versus placebo (2.1%). The majority of fractures observed in female patients were nonvertebral fractures including lower limb and distal upper limb.
signal_headline: Pioglitazone was associated with a higher fracture incidence in women in PROactive
signal_summary: Women 5.1% (44/870) vs placebo 2.5% (23/905) · Men 1.7% vs 2.1% · mean follow-up 34.5 months
why_it_matters: The prescribing information identifies a fracture signal in women that was not observed in men in the same way.
cautions: Not every woman receiving pioglitazone will experience a fracture
No mechanism is inferred beyond the source

endpoint: Next-morning impairment and sex-specific drug elimination
effect_measure: Regulatory dosing action based on sex-specific drug elimination
interpretation: The FDA reported that women eliminate zolpidem more slowly than men and may have next-morning blood levels high enough to impair activities requiring alertness. FDA required lower recommended initial doses for women: immediate-release products from 10 mg to 5 mg, and extended-release products from 12.5 mg to 6.25 mg. Product-specific dosing differs across formulations; this is regulatory dosing information, not individual prescribing advice. This is an example where sex-specific evidence directly changed regulatory dosing information.
exact_passage: Because women eliminate zolpidem from their bodies more slowly than men, and data show that blood levels in some patients may be high enough the morning after use to impair activities that require alertness, including driving, FDA is requiring the manufacturers to lower the recommended dose of zolpidem for women: for immediate-release products (Ambien, Edluar, and Zolpimist) the recommended dose for women is lowered from 10 mg to 5 mg, and for extended-release products (Ambien CR) from 12.5 mg to 6.25 mg.
signal_headline: FDA lowered recommended zolpidem doses for women after evidence of slower elimination and next-morning impairment risk
signal_summary: Immediate-release: 10 mg → 5 mg for women · Extended-release: 12.5 mg → 6.25 mg for women
why_it_matters: This is an example where sex-specific evidence directly changed regulatory dosing information.
cautions: Regulatory dosing information, not individual prescribing advice
Does not establish an individual patient's outcome

effect_measure: Relative risk (aspirin vs placebo, women only)
interpretation: In the Women's Health Study, a women-only randomized trial of 39,876 initially healthy women, low-dose aspirin (100 mg every other day over 10 years) produced a nonsignificant 9% reduction in the primary major cardiovascular endpoint (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.80-1.03, P=0.13). Aspirin had no significant effect on myocardial infarction (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.84-1.25, P=0.83) or cardiovascular death (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.74-1.22, P=0.68). Because the trial enrolled only women, it does not compare the treatment effect between women and men.
exact_passage: 477 major cardiovascular events were confirmed in the aspirin group, as compared with 522 in the placebo group, for a nonsignificant reduction in risk with aspirin of 9 percent (relative risk, 0.91; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.80 to 1.03; P=0.13).

effect_measure: Relative risk (aspirin vs placebo, women only)
interpretation: In the women-only Women's Health Study, low-dose aspirin reduced the risk of stroke by 17% (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.69-0.99, P=0.04), driven by a 24% reduction in ischemic stroke (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63-0.93, P=0.009). These are within-trial outcomes in women; the trial did not compare the effect between women and men.
exact_passage: there was a 17 percent reduction in the risk of stroke in the aspirin group, as compared with the placebo group (relative risk, 0.83; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.69 to 0.99; P=0.04), owing to a 24 percent reduction in the risk of ischemic stroke (relative risk, 0.76; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.63 to 0.93; P=0.009).

effect_measure: Relative risk (aspirin vs placebo, women only)
interpretation: In the women-only Women's Health Study, gastrointestinal bleeding requiring transfusion was more frequent with low-dose aspirin than placebo (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.07-1.83, P=0.02). This is a within-trial safety outcome in women; it is not a between-sex comparison and not a treatment recommendation.
exact_passage: Gastrointestinal bleeding requiring transfusion was more frequent in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (relative risk, 1.40; 95 percent confidence interval, 1.07 to 1.83; P=0.02).
